section_summary: This section documents diplomatic discussions and State Department policy formulation between April and May 1948 regarding the Japanese Maritime Safety Authorities Bill establishing the Maritime Safety Board. It details U.S. efforts to resist Far Eastern Commission (FEC) intervention and Allied objections—principally from the British, Soviets, New Zealanders, and Chinese concerning vessel size, armaments, and jurisdiction over foreign ships—while upholding SCAP's independent authority to allow Japan to police its coastal waters against smuggling and illegal immigration. The documents include memoranda of conversations with Allied diplomats, instructions to the U.S. FEC representative, reports on Steering Committee meetings, copies of SCAP technical communications, and the Japanese statutory text of Law No. 35.

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton informs Canadian Second Secretary Ralph E. Collins of the U.S. position opposing Far Eastern Commission interference with the Japanese Maritime Safety Authorities Bill and restricting conference attendance to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: Borton stated that the U.S. opposed asking SCAP to withhold passage of the maritime bill and considered water police normal and necessary. Collins reported Canada had no objections to the bill but queried whether patrol boat armaments violated disarmament policy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Telephone Conversation with Ralph E. Collins on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill and Conference Attendance

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton conveys the U.S. position on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill and inter-governmental conference attendance to Netherlands Minister O. Reuchlin.
subfiles.summary: Borton affirmed that the U.S. opposed delaying the maritime safety legislation. Reuchlin, as Steering Committee Chairman, agreed to report the bill was under consideration to minimize debate, understanding Japan's need for maritime safety while noting earlier information would have aided Allied acceptance.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Telephone Conversation with O. Reuchlin on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill and Conference Attendance

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton discusses the U.S. stance on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill with Chinese Minister Plenipotentiary Dr. Shao-Hwa Tan.
subfiles.summary: Borton conveyed U.S. opposition to FEC attempts to block the maritime safety bill. Addressing Tan's concern over the 1,500-ton vessel provision, Borton explained that the total 50,000-ton ceiling across 125 vessels ensured the fleet would predominantly consist of smaller craft.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Telephone Conversation with Dr. Shao-Hwa Tan on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton meets with French Embassy official Paul Guerin to explain U.S. policies regarding the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill and Japanese attendance at technical conferences.
subfiles.summary: Borton outlined U.S. opposition to delaying the bill and explained policy limiting international conference attendance to SCAP. Guerin reported French sympathy for anti-smuggling patrols but noted legal concerns that vessel armament might conflict with FEC disarmament policy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Paul Guerin on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill and Conference Attendance

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton informs Australian Second Secretary H. W. Bullock of the U.S. position on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill.
subfiles.summary: Borton stated the U.S. opposed FEC intervention delaying the bill. Bullock responded that inquiries in Tokyo had largely satisfied Australia, though concern remained over potential naval armament on patrol vessels.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Telephone Conversation with H. W. Bullock on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton communicates the U.S. stance opposing Far Eastern Commission delay of the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill to British Counselor Hubert Graves.
subfiles.summary: Borton conveyed U.S. opposition to consultative messages delaying the bill. Graves suggested placing the burden on the Soviets to demonstrate any conflict with FEC policy decisions; conference attendance was not discussed.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Telephone Conversation with Hubert Graves on the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill and Conference Attendance

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary Charles E. Saltzman transmits SCAP's reply regarding the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill to Far Eastern Commission Chairman General Frank R. McCoy for circulation.
subfiles.summary: Cover memorandum forwarding SCAP's factual reply concerning the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill for circulation to the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of SCAP Reply on Maritime Safety Authorities Bill to Far Eastern Commission

subfiles.about: SCAP provides a nine-point factual statement clarifying the scope, personnel, armaments, and anti-smuggling purpose of the newly enacted Maritime Safety Authorities Bill.
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: Clarifies that the bill passed the Diet on April 15 to suppress smuggling, authorizes 720 shipboard personnel carrying sidearms but no vessel armament, and limits vessels to 125 under SCAP supervision.
subfiles.title: SCAP Statement of Facts Concerning the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary Charles E. Saltzman instructs the U.S. Member on the Far Eastern Commission to oppose any proposal prohibiting or delaying the Japanese Maritime Safety Authority.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman instructs the U.S. Member to oppose New Zealand's proposal delaying coastal patrol implementation. He stresses supporting SCAP's independent authority, asserting that the bill conforms with FEC disarmament policies, and resisting an unnecessary FEC policy decision.
subfiles.title: Instructions for the United States Member, Far Eastern Commission: Maritime Safety Authorities Bill
subfiles.to: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton reports to W. Walton Butterworth on Steering Committee proceedings regarding the Japanese coastal patrol, industrial levels, and conference attendance.
subfiles.summary: Reports the Steering Committee's adoption (5 to 1) of New Zealand's coastal patrol paper over U.S. opposition, defeat of a Soviet amendment, discussions on technological information and Japanese conference attendance, and Canadian views on patrol vessel armaments.
subfiles.title: Report on FEC Steering Committee Meeting of April 27, 1948

subfiles.about: The United States Government submits its formal views arguing against the New Zealand policy proposal to postpone the Japanese coastal patrol legislation.
subfiles.summary: Maintains that establishing maritime safety authorities is proper for the Diet and certified by SCAP as consistent with FEC policies. Argues that delaying enacted Japanese legislation exceeds FEC competence and constitutes improper administrative interference.
subfiles.title: Japanese Coastal Patrol (SC-305/8): Views of the U.S. Government on Policy Proposal Submitted by the New Zealand Representative

subfiles.about: W. Walton Butterworth recommends that the Under Secretary of State reject a British diplomatic request to instruct SCAP to postpone promulgation of the Maritime Safety Authorities Law.
subfiles.summary: Recommends refusing British diplomatic requests to postpone the law's May 1 promulgation following an American veto of a New Zealand FEC proposal, arguing that SCAP independence should be upheld in line with the Kennan report.
subfiles.title: British Request that United States Government Instruct SCAP to Postpone Promulgation of Japanese Maritime Safety Authorities Law

subfiles.about: John M. Allison records a discussion with British Counselor Hubert A. Graves regarding British objections to the Japanese Maritime Safety Authorities Law and its pending promulgation.
subfiles.summary: Graves expressed British concern over vessel speed, tonnage, and search powers over foreign ships, urging diplomatic postponement. Allison defended SCAP's supervisory authority and noted that the law posed no security threat to Allied powers.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Hubert A. Graves on Japanese Maritime Safety Authorities Law

subfiles.about: The Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan transmits two copies of the official Japanese text of the Maritime Safety Authority Law.
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.summary: Transmits two copies of the Japanese text of the Maritime Safety Authority Law enacted by the Diet.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 269: Transmitting Japanese Text of Maritime Safety Authority Law

subfiles.about: The official Japanese legislative text of Law No. 35 establishing the Maritime Safety Authority under the Ministry of Transportation.
subfiles.summary: This statute enacts Law No. 35 establishing the Maritime Safety Authority as an external agency of the Ministry of Transportation to maintain maritime order, navigational aids, and sea rescue. It establishes the organizational structure, administrative apparatus, and authority of the Director-General and maritime safety officials. Additionally, it designates maritime safety officials as judicial police officers, regulates inter-agency cooperation, and sets forth supplementary and transitional provisions.
subfiles.title: Maritime Safety Authority Law (Law No. 35 of 1948)

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary Charles E. Saltzman transmits an English translation of the enacted Maritime Safety Authority Law, outlining minor text corrections and confirming its May 1 implementation.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman forwards an English translation of the enacted law to the U.S. Member for FEC distribution, notes specific wording changes and typographical corrections made from draft SC 305/1, and confirms SCAP implemented the law on May 1.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the United States Member, Far Eastern Commission: Maritime Safety Authority Bill
subfiles.to: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary Charles E. Saltzman forwards additional information from SCAP regarding the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill to the U.S. Member on the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: Cover memorandum forwarding an additional SCAP explanatory message regarding the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill for Far Eastern Commission information.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of Additional SCAP Information Concerning Maritime Safety Authorities Bill
subfiles.to: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission

subfiles.about: SCAP provides detailed operational and technical data on vessel tonnage, speed limits, search jurisdiction, and demobilization personnel under the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill.
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: Details fleet restrictions including 1,500-ton maximum and 15 knots speed, planning for 125 vessels, SCAP authority over searches of foreign vessels under SCAP-INs, prohibition of former military career officers except for minesweeping, and cost savings for the occupation.
subfiles.title: SCAP Explanatory Message Regarding the Maritime Safety Authorities Bill
